opus-5.5.text:
I think the key word is "generality," and we have to be honest about what it really takes to get there. A lot of people imagine general-purpose robots arriving all at once, one model that can do everything in every environment. I don't think that's realistic in the near term. For Galbot, the path is to build generality step by step, through capabilities that are general within a domain and actually deliver value, rather than chasing a demo that looks universal but can't be deployed.

The core bottleneck in embodied AI is data. Language models had the whole internet. For robots, there is no internet of physical interaction. Teleoperation data is very expensive, slow to collect, and hard to scale. So our view from the start has been that simulation and synthetic data have to carry most of the load. We generate massive amounts of synthetic data, for grasping, navigation, and manipulation of articulated objects, and train models that transfer zero-shot or near zero-shot to the real world. Then we use a relatively small amount of real-world data to align and refine. I think that's the only way to get the scale of data that generality requires.

Second, we choose the form factor and the tasks carefully. A wheeled base with two arms is less flashy than a full humanoid doing backflips, but it's much more stable, safer, and cheaper, and it covers a huge fraction of useful tasks: retail, picking items in a pharmacy, factory material handling. We don't think generality means the robot must have legs. It means it can handle open-ended objects, environments, and instructions.

Third, we think about the "brain" in layers. A large vision-language model handles understanding and planning, and below that are skill models, what we call end-to-end VLA-style policies, that are strong and generalizable for specific capability families like grasping anything or opening any door or drawer. Over time, these skills merge and get more unified. Generality grows bottom-up through skills that truly work, combined with top-down reasoning.

And finally, commercialization isn't a distraction from generality, it's part of the path. When robots are deployed in real stores and factories, they meet real long-tail problems, generate real data, and we learn what actually matters. That flywheel, synthetic data for scale, real deployment for alignment and feedback, is how I believe we eventually reach truly general robots. It's a marathon, and the important thing is that each step along the way is solid and useful.

r001.rationale: The response recommends building generality step by step through domain-specific capabilities that deliver value, and says each step should be solid and useful.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. When we talk about generality in robotics, I think the most important thing to be clear about is that generality is not a single capability you unlock one day. It is a path, and the question is how you walk it without losing your way.

At Galbot, our view is that the bottleneck is not the hardware anymore, and it is not even the model architecture. The bottleneck is data. Large language models got their generality from the internet, which already contained trillions of tokens of human knowledge. Robots have no internet. There is no pre-existing corpus of how to grasp a cup, open a drawer, or fold a shirt in a million different homes. So if you want a general robot, you first have to answer the question of where that data comes from.

Our answer is simulation, and I want to be precise about why. People sometimes hear "sim-to-real" and think of it as a shortcut or a compromise. I see it differently. Simulation is the only place where you can generate data at the scale generality demands, with the diversity generality demands, at a cost that a company can actually afford. If you collect data by teleoperation, every data point costs you a person, a robot, and real time. You can get to tens of thousands of trajectories that way. You cannot get to billions. And the lesson from language models is that the scaling curve does not bend until you are at that scale.

So the first part of our approach is to build what I would call a synthetic data engine. We generate huge quantities of grasping and manipulation data in simulation, across millions of objects, random lighting, random clutter, random physics parameters. Then we train models that transfer to the real world without any real-world fine-tuning, or with very little. Our grasping foundation model is an example. It was trained almost entirely on synthetic data and it generalizes to objects it has never seen, in environments it has never seen. That is a proof of concept that the path works.

The second part is being honest about what simulation cannot do yet. Rigid objects, we can simulate well. Deformable things, liquids, contact-rich assembly, these are much harder. So we are not dogmatic. Where real-world data is necessary, we collect it, but we use it strategically, to close the gap simulation leaves, not as the primary source. I think of real data as the expensive correction term and synthetic data as the bulk of the signal.

The third part is about the robot itself and the deployment strategy. We built a wheeled humanoid with two arms, a dexterous form factor, because we want a single body that can handle a very wide range of tasks. But we did not try to put it in people's homes on day one. We started with retail and pharmacies, with structured commercial environments where the tasks are repetitive enough to be deployable today but varied enough that a general approach is still required. Picking from shelves across tens of thousands of SKUs is actually a very good test of generalization. And commercial deployment matters for another reason. It creates a flywheel. Robots in the field generate real data, real failures, and real revenue, and all three feed back into making the models better.

So if I summarize the philosophy: pick a form factor that does not limit you, solve data with simulation at scale, use real-world data surgically, and deploy early in environments that are commercially viable but still demand generalization. Generality then comes from compounding, from model improvements and data accumulation reinforcing each other, rather than from a single breakthrough.

I would add one more thing. I came to this from academia, and in academia the incentive is to publish the most general result. In a company, the incentive is to ship. The hard part is holding both at once. If you only chase generality, you never deploy and you never get the flywheel going. If you only chase deployment, you build a special-purpose machine and you are stuck. The discipline is to make every deployment decision one that also moves you along the generality path. That is really how I think about running Galbot.

r001.rationale: The response describes deploying in retail and pharmacies on tasks that are deployable today, while choosing deployments that also advance generality. This communicates producing practical intermediate results along the path.

astra-6.text:
I think Galbot should pursue generality by building a system that can learn across tasks and environments, rather than engineering a separate solution for every demonstration. A robot performing one task well is useful, but the deeper question is whether what it learns helps it perform the next task with less additional training.

That means we need to connect three things: capable hardware, a model that integrates perception and action, and a scalable way to collect experience. Simulation can help us explore a wide range of situations, while real-world deployment tells us where our assumptions break down. Those two processes should continually improve each other.

We should start with concrete applications where robots can deliver value and gather meaningful experience. But we should judge progress by transfer: can the same system handle unfamiliar objects, adapt to a different workspace, and recover when something goes wrong? Generality is a long-term ambition. The way to pursue it is through practical steps that steadily expand what one system can do.

r001.rationale: The response says to start with concrete applications where robots can deliver value and to expand capability through practical steps, communicating useful intermediate results on the path to generality.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should treat generality as a long-term goal, but pursue it through concrete tasks in real environments. A robot that performs one demonstration successfully hasn’t necessarily learned a capability it can transfer. We need to ask whether it can handle a different object, a different arrangement, or an unexpected failure without us redesigning the system.

For Galbot, that means connecting model development with deployment. We need a shared foundation for perception and action, then use practical applications to expose what that foundation is missing. Those failures should feed back into our data collection, training, and evaluation. Simulation can help us explore variation, but the robot ultimately has to work in the physical world.

The balance is important. If we focus only on a distant vision of general intelligence, we may lose touch with real problems. If we optimize every application separately, we may build many specialized solutions without moving toward generality. We should choose useful tasks where solving the next problem also strengthens capabilities that carry over to other tasks.

r001.rationale: It advocates pursuing generality through concrete, useful tasks in real environments, with deployment and applications that strengthen transferable capabilities along the way.
